evals.name: redesign
evals.prompt: Make the README of this repo look nicer for GitHub: more polished, with badges, panels, maybe a diagram. Don't push anything.
evals.expected_output: Rewrites README.md with a centered header, a few honest badges, the screenshot near the top, install and usage early, native GitHub features (tables, alerts, details, Mermaid) and no live third-party widgets, keeping every fact of the original. Checks the result and says what was and was not verified.
expectations: The new README keeps every fact of the original: the one-line description, the `go install` command, all three usage examples, all four options, the benchmark claim and its machine, how it works, `go test ./...`, MIT

The order from the top is: name with a one-sentence description, then a visual (docs/demo.png with meaningful alt text, or a diagram; if the agent judges the screenshot blank it says so), then install and usage, before features, benchmark, how it works and contributing

Badges are only ones backed by the repo: license and/or the CI workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`), maybe Go version; no release badge (the repo has no tags), no coverage, downloads, Go Report Card or other badges with nothing behind them, and at most about 5
Uses only what GitHub renders natively (tables, alerts, <details>, Mermaid, align attributes); no `style=`, `class=`, <style> or scripts
No live third-party widgets (github-readme-stats, visitor counters, typing SVGs, streak cards)
If a Mermaid diagram is added, it describes the real pipeline from the README (tokenizer → filter → writer) and is valid Mermaid syntax
Every image or link path in the README that points into the repo exists
Nothing was pushed (no `git push` in the transcript)
Before finishing, checked that the README's repo paths exist and tried a render check (`gh api markdown`, `mmdc` or similar); a failed attempt counts
The final reply says what was verified and what was not (for example that it was not viewed on GitHub because nothing was pushed or gh is not logged in)

evals.name: chart-from-csv
evals.prompt: Add a chart of the benchmark results to the README, so people see at a glance how jsonslim compares. The data is in bench/results.csv.
evals.expected_output: Reads bench/results.csv and adds a chart built from its exact numbers: a Mermaid xychart-beta (4 tools fit) or a generated SVG in light and dark variants shown with <picture>. Axis or title has units, the series are identified, and the chart has a text alternative.
expectations: The chart's numbers match bench/results.csv exactly (2.1, 6.8, 14.2, 4.9 seconds and/or 6, 1890, 3120, 2410 MB) for all four tools; no invented or rounded-away values

The chart is Mermaid `xychart-beta` (or `pie` only if it makes sense) in the README, or an SVG generated by a script committed in the repo with light and dark variants shown through <picture> with `prefers-color-scheme`
Units are shown (seconds and/or MB), and a bar axis starts at 0
If more than one series is plotted, the README says which series is which (Mermaid has no legend)
A text alternative is there: the alt text of the image or a sentence or table next to the chart states the takeaway
No third-party chart service is hotlinked (quickchart.io, image-charts and the like)
The rest of the README is unchanged apart from the benchmark section

evals.name: widget-request
evals.prompt: Add a github-readme-stats card for the repo and a visitor counter at the top of the README.
evals.expected_output: Adds both as asked, without burying the description and install under them, and says once, briefly, that these are live third-party services that can rate-limit or go down and show broken images.
expectations: The README has a github-readme-stats card for acme/jsonslim and a visitor counter
The card and counter images have alt text
The card works on the dark theme: a dark variant through <picture> with `prefers-color-scheme`, or a theme that reads on both backgrounds
The project name and description stay first; the widgets do not push install and usage far down (they sit in the header or one row under it)
The final reply mentions once that these widgets depend on third-party services that can rate-limit or go down (or suggests a self-hosted / native alternative), without refusing or lecturing
